questions.q: Why does a confirmed malicious finding from a hunting query create an ongoing gap if nothing further is done?
options: A hunting query only runs when an analyst manually re-runs it, so the same pattern won't be caught automatically next time
Hunting queries can only ever be run once per workspace
Sentinel automatically deletes hunting query results after 24 hours
A confirmed finding automatically becomes a new incident with no further action needed
questions.explain: Because a hunting query is on-demand, not scheduled, the same real pattern goes uncaught unless someone manually hunts for it again.

questions.q: What is the practical first step in converting a successful hunt into a permanent detection?
options: Deleting the original hunting query so it can't be run again
Filing a help desk ticket with no technical details attached
Taking the proven KQL query, or a lightly refined version, into Sentinel's Create Scheduled query rule flow
Waiting for Microsoft to add the pattern to the built-in rule template gallery
questions.explain: The hunt already produced a proven KQL query — turning it into a Scheduled Analytics Rule reuses that same logic under Analytics > Create.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what usually needs the most deliberate attention when converting a hunt's query into a scheduled rule?
options: Whether the query uses KQL or a different language entirely
The scheduling settings — run frequency, lookback window, and alert threshold
The lesson's narration script, which must be rewritten entirely
The color scheme of the Sentinel dashboard
questions.explain: The query logic already proved itself; what needs tuning is how often it runs, how far back it looks, and what threshold triggers an alert.

questions.q: Why should the lookback window on the new scheduled rule be set longer than its run frequency, per the Sentinel course guidance this lesson references?
options: Because a shorter lookback window always produces more false positives
Because Sentinel requires the lookback window to always equal 24 hours
To make the rule run less frequently overall
To avoid missing events caught in an ingestion-delay gap between two scheduled runs
questions.explain: Log ingestion isn't instantaneous, so a lookback window longer than the run frequency avoids an event falling between two scheduled runs.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the real difference between a SOC that hunts occasionally and one where hunting measurably improves the baseline?
options: Confirmed hunts get converted into scheduled rules, so the same gap in detection coverage stays permanently closed
The second SOC only uses built-in rule templates and never writes custom queries
The second SOC never performs hypothesis-driven hunting at all
There is no real difference — both approaches produce identical detection coverage
questions.explain: Converting confirmed hunt findings into scheduled rules is what makes hunting cumulatively improve detection coverage rather than stay a one-off exercise.
